title: One rule per element vs three competing rules resolved by !important
variable: 200 plain rules vs 600 overlapping rules with !important overrides
claim: Antipattern #30 from web-performance-antipatterns-50.md: '!important and specificity wars producing redundant overriding rules that all still match.' The cost claimed here is not parsing but matching: a losing rule is still a rule the engine had to find, match and then discard. Every long-lived stylesheet accumulates these, and unlike an oversized stylesheet the extra rules DO match the elements on screen, so indexing cannot skip them.
result: CONFIRMED: Styles 1.93x / 1.95x / 2.03x, essentially flat in element count. Tripling the rules that match each element - with the winner decided by !important rather than by order - roughly doubles styling time. This is the counterpart to stylesheet-size-200-vs-5000: rules that match NOTHING are free, rules that match and then lose are not. A specificity war is paid on every restyle of every element it touches.
notes: Applicability gate: DIRECT. Rule 1: one variable, whether each element is matched by one rule or by three competing ones. Rule 2: identical DOM, same tiles, same classes. The final rendered colour is the same in both variants - B's chain is constructed so the !important winner lands on the same colour A's single rule produces, so the pixels match and only the resolution work differs. Rule 3: identical JS, byte-for-byte. Rule 4: no text, no assets. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the class churn IS the case and replaces the shared damage driver, so the cascade is resolved afresh every frame. Rule 7: no randomness. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300 elements against 200 vs 600 rules. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Styles. NOTE: this differs from stylesheet-size-200-vs-5000 in the way that matters - there the extra rules match NOTHING on the page, here every extra rule matches a real element and must be resolved against its competitors. Comparing the two rows separates 'a big stylesheet' from 'a contested cascade'. Generated by tools/make-rule-heavy-cases.js.
